content: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a potential complication that can occur in women who take certain fertility medications designed to stimulate egg production. Symptoms of OHSS: The symptoms of OHSS can vary in severity, ranging from mild to severe. Mild symptoms may include: Abdominal bloating Mild abdominal pain Weight gain Severe symptoms, though rare, may include: Significant weight gain (more than 10 pounds within 3–5 days) Severe abdominal pain or swelling Decreased urination Shortness of breath Causes of OHSS: Under normal circumstances, a woman produces one egg per month. Fertility treatments often involve medications to regulate or increase egg production. However, if these drugs overstimulate the ovaries, the ovaries can become swollen, and fluid may leak into the abdominal and chest cavities. This condition is known as ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). OHSS typically occurs after ovulation, when the eggs are released from the ovaries. The risk of OHSS increases if a hormone injection called human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is used to trigger ovulation. The risk is even higher if multiple doses of hCG are administered after ovulation or if pregnancy occurs during the same cycle. OHSS is rare in women who only take oral fertility medications. Up to 10% of women undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) may develop OHSS, with most cases being mild. However, some women may experience a severe and potentially dangerous form of OHSS. Additional risk factors for OHSS include: Being younger than 35 years old Having very high estrogen levels during fertility treatments Having polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: You should contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience any of the following symptoms: Excessive weight gain (more than 5 pounds in a single day) Severe abdominal pain Intense nausea that prevents you from keeping food or liquids down Decreased urination Shortness of breath Dizziness Diagnosis: In severe cases of OHSS, your healthcare provider will closely monitor your symptoms. Hospitalization may be required. Your weight and abdominal size will be measured regularly. Diagnostic tests may include: Abdominal or vaginal ultrasound Chest X-ray Complete blood count (CBC) Electrolyte panel Liver function tests Tests to measure urine output Treatment Options: Mild cases of OHSS often resolve without specific treatment. To alleviate discomfort, you can: Rest with your legs elevated to help your body release excess fluid. However, light activity is generally better than complete bed rest unless otherwise advised by your doctor. Drink at least 10–12 glasses of fluids daily, especially those containing electrolytes. Avoid alcohol and caffeinated beverages (e.g., coffee, colas). Refrain from intense exercise and sexual intercourse, as these activities can exacerbate ovarian discomfort, potentially leading to ovarian cyst rupture, fluid leakage, or ovarian torsion (twisting of the ovary that cuts off blood flow). Use over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen (Tylenol). Weigh yourself daily to monitor for excessive weight gain (5 or more pounds in a day). Severe cases of OHSS may require hospitalization. In such cases, healthcare providers may: Administer intravenous (IV) fluids Remove excess fluid that has accumulated in the body Closely monitor your condition Prognosis: Most mild cases of OHSS resolve on their own after menstruation begins. Severe cases may take several days to improve. If pregnancy occurs during OHSS, symptoms may worsen and could take weeks to resolve. Possible Complications: In rare cases, OHSS can lead to life-threatening complications, including: Blood clots Kidney failure Severe electrolyte imbalances Significant fluid accumulation in the abdomen or chest Prevention: If you are receiving fertility injections, your doctor will monitor you closely with blood tests and pelvic ultrasounds to ensure your ovaries are not over-responding. Rapid or excessive increases in estrogen levels during fertility treatments increase the risk of OHSS. In such cases, your doctor may lower the medication dose or temporarily stop treatment. Some women may be given a protein solution called albumin to reduce the likelihood of developing OHSS.
